newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico's governor expected to stay in office.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico's governor expected to stay in office.

text.p: Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello was expected to retain office as voters on this Caribbean island went to the polls Tuesday.

Elections are loud, colourful and passionate on the Spanish-speaking U.S. Commonwealth of 3.6 million people. Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens but do not vote in national elections or pay federal taxes.
Late opinion polls showed Rossello leading his rival Hector Luis Acevedo by 52 to 36 percent.

At stake in the election is the entire government of Puerto Rico -- the governorship, all the seats in its bicameral legislature, its non-voting delegate to the U.S. Congress and mayors' and municipal assembly seats in all 78 of its municipalities.
This year crime and government corruption were issues but as always they were overshadowed by Puerto Rico's perennial quandry -- its relationship with the United States.

Rossello and his New Progressive Party favour U.S. statehood for Puerto Rico. Acevedo and the Popular Democratic Party seek to maintain the commonwealth status, which they bill as "Lo mejor de dos mundos" -- the best of both worlds.
The Independence Party, which seeks to set up the Republic of Puerto Rico, is a small but vocal minority. Its gubernatorial candidate David Noriega is not expected to be a factor in the race.
In a 1993 referendum, 48 per cent of Puerto Rican voters chose commonwealth staus, 46 per cent opted for statehood and the remainder chose independence.

In the weeks leading up to the vote, caravans of political candidates and their supporters clogged roads and city streets. Sound trucks stacked high with speakers cruised neighbourhoods and blasted campaign jingles at top volume.
